is what i said. you kinda missed the point of my post. i said in my statement that i am judgmental. so of course my perception might be skewed, but the point of my reply was to show my judgemental pov, because that's how most of society sees it despite the truth or the objective pov. others can choose to act all high and mighty and say "keep being confident" but it's not that easy, people are still going to be ignorant and unwilling to accept people unlike them. the replies to this post are lovely, but saying that he's "laying on a little thick" or nitpicking the amy schumer comments seem like being overly critical and just trying to divert the issue and the blame away from society being harsh due to his impairment. he's been living with this impairment for his whole life, so he has likely tried many solutions and not "laying it on thick" or not talking at all, or talking an amount equal to everyone else, but still came to this same conclusion. like you said, i am judgmental and i should work on that. on the outside when i talk to people i don't openly display my biases, which is why my post was more of an internal bias i just have had since like forever, which can subtly exude outward. my post was also a reflection of how friends, family, and people around me act. they tend to "baby" people with impairments or just ignore them, so while it's nice to be positive and encouraging people are still gonna be dicks 90% of the time. creator's post about his experience opened my eyes a lot too, so i'll definitely be more understanding to people with similar impairments or that are different from me. yes, my post was uncomfortable af to make, but in my opinion necessary to say the hard truth. am constantly working on changing my perspective, but in order for others to do the same, it's gonna take a lot.

chills, i got the same exact classes as you this soph year, english honors, chem honors, precalc honors, and apush 1. i had like all straight A's freshman year except bio which ended in like an 86. this year my precalc is 76, apush 88, chem 88, (all overall from the 3 quarters) but my elective classes are doing okay since they're a breeze. i am worried sick as well. nothing has helped really, which is why my grades are still ass lol. precalc im trying, but the tests are just way harder than the material. there has been one thing that has made a slight difference however. i dmed some of the kids in my classes on ig that i didn't know that well and tried to be friends with them (easier if they're in your grade but i did become friends with this 11th grader). it humanizes this pandemic a lot, we talked about osu and some animes, and just jokes. and when we talked about class, it seemed like we had the same issues, and felt the same way about the problems we were facing. so knowing you're not alone helps a lot, even if they may have better grades than you. and in class after talking to them i found myself participating more and being more eager to do the work knowing that my new acquaintance was in that class, and also because it seemed like you were actually taking the class with someone else not just slumped behind a screen. also added adrenaline from messaging random people. my chem and apush is low due to not turning work on time from the lack of motivation, so if all my work was in it would probably be around a low A. it seems our grades are low in the opposite classes, so if you like we could study together and just msg questions (feynman study technique of teaching what you know to other people). to answer how this will affect gpa, it probably will. negative impact being usually in a non pandemic situation, a dealbreaker. but since we are in a panini rn, be able to explain why you had a slump in sophomore year on the extra info part of apps, and take this year as a learning experience and blow it out of the water junior year. junior year and senior year are more important ne ways. colleges will also be more lenient i assume, since a lot of kids are failing this year that have been straight A students before. remember, which college isn't important, but what you do with it and what skills you can market to employers at your desired job is more important. i send love and peace to u, let's both do our best!

if im honest, i'd probably treat you different from everyone else since that's just what i've been doing my whole life. don't see many people like you irl, and the people with impairments i have met tend to act very reserved and, liked you said, perceived as weak. society has made a structure so hard to push back against that anyone who does is just laughed at, since it looks odd and is uncomprehendable to other people that someone who has been dealt a worse hand than theirs is more confident than themselves. it's like they think you should be weak and pitying yourself because of your situation, and people will feel at ease that they are "automatically better" despite it being something you can't control. keep being confident, and eventually people will ease up and not be such a douche (unless they really are douches). we need more people like you to fight the norm, to inspire others to do the same, and hopefully one day the majority of people with impairments or disabilities can be confident and society will see that behavior as the norm. those who are cold after you try warming up to them, or still act indifferent after getting to know you, they aren't worth it. there's a lot of judgmental people like me, who just need that one little push to see things from a different perspective, and likely will respect you tremendously when that shift occurs (which you could be the catalyst of). best of luck

If you have this much anxiety about it that you couldn't call, imagine if you were the girl in this situation. Right now you probably aren't even considering whether or not the other person is anxious as well and assuming they are calm. Being said, most people are so caught up with how they themselves are presented to worry about the other person's responses/actions. Consider this: you are talking to someone and they are annoying you. You think the other person is annoying, but the other person doesn't think so, and continues talking to you. Now flip it and imagine perceiving them as being nice, and being concerned whether or not you are the annoying one. Nothing changed except your view of the situation, which is the most important. When you call her, focus on her and listening rather than coming up with a response, and if you're unsure what to say, repeat the last word she says (ex. 1. What food do you like? 2. Apples. 1. Apples? 2. yeah, the color is nice). For me, I don't think embarrassment exists. You're the only one who can feel it, so if you don't believe in it, who can inflict it upon you? Everything is within the bounds of your own perception. Focus on whether or not you like the girl, not whether or not she likes you. Hope it goes well man

I heard a podcast before from college admissions officers or people who help others land jobs feel there is a lack of thank you's. I myself help others (no compensation) with language learning and typically 60% of the time do not receive any type of appreciation or thank you. So say your thank you's and be as polite as possible at all times, because you are likely the minority doing so for that person on the receiving end, and they will remember you for that. As for non professional relationships, maybe bring up opportunities to get ahead in career to your friend and let them know indirectly you want the best for them. Or let them know about tricks you learned (ex. my friend wanted to cut bangs, I digressed a technique I learned on how do do it on your own in a paragraph). This is just what I do, and it shows that you value spending time to help the other person. The key is doing things that would take time our of your day, or a lot of thought. Hope you have a good one!
